newsitem.title: UK: Stoiber comment boosts recovering mark further.
newsitem.headline: Stoiber comment boosts recovering mark further.

text.p: The mark edged higher against its European counterparts in morning trade, boosted by renewed anxiety about the future of European monetary union amid rifts between German political leaders on the issue.
The mark was also buoyant on the crosses thanks to its recovery against other major currencies, clawing up from the multi-year lows it fell to versus the dollar and sterling late last week.

Edmund Stoiber, premier of the German state of Bavaria, reawakened EMU anxiety by saying in Monday's edition of Britain's Financial Times that a delay in EMU would be better than a weak single currency.

Bavarian finance minister Erwin Huber added to Stoiber's severity, saying monetary union could be launched without France -- seen as a "core" EMU candidate country alongside Germany -- if Paris did not meet the criteria.
France has already admitted it would overshoot the budget deficit-to-GDP target ratio of three percent this year.

Stoiber's remark was almost identical to what he had said one week ago, and while today's comment appeared to worry the market a bit more, traders said it was not creating many waves in the mark crosses.

"The Stoiber comment's has given the mark a slight boost, as you might expect, and though mark/lira's up more than a big figure and a half, it's not all that exciting," said one trader at a Japanese bank. "But it does show there's unease in Germany."
Traders said signs of a cooling off in the Italian government bond market, which had a record-breaking bull run last week, might also have prompted softness in the lira.

The mark was at 975.45/65 lire at 0940 GMT, just off its morining high, and up from 973.05/35 in late Europe on Friday. Mark/Paris was at 3.3707/12 against 3.3694/99, with traders saying they were not particularly worried by Huber's comment.
Analysts said Stoiber's recent rhetoric appeared to be based more on political intentions rather than economic reality in view of German elections next year.

"The debate is heating up within Germany itself, which suggests that the politicians are drawing EMU more into the political arena," said Elizabeth Legge, senior economist at Bankgesellschaft Berlin here.

"EMU doesn't have all that much backing in the country, and it's going to be a great temptation for them to use that (EMU scepticism) as a way of winning votes, although no-one is willing to come right out and say...'no' to EMU," Legge said.
European finance and economic ministers were expected to use their regular meeting in Brussels today as an opportunity to soothe market nerves made jittery by Stoiber's remarks.
"The Ecofin meeting's likely to be the more of the usual smoothing-over process, and otherwise we're not expecting all that much from it," the bank trader said.

The meeting was also due to discuss Italy's economic convergence plans to qualify for the single currency, which foresees a budget deficit of 3.0 percent of GDP for this year and 2.8 in 1998. According to the plan, GDP is expected to grow by 1.2 percent this year and 2.0 in 1998.

Jean-Claude Juncker, prime minister of Luxembourg which currently holds the EU presidency, said on Monday that Italy's convergence plans clearly showed the nation was moving in a good direction, although he added that Rome needed to do more work on its economy.
"Italy's convergence plan should go down rather well. The Italians seem to be making a good deal of progress and they've got some support from Brussels," Bankgesellschaft's Legge said.

"There's good reason to criticise some of the things they've done (concerning EMU convergence) but they should get a kind hearing at the Ecofin meeting as there's a general idea that they've worked very hard."
